teaser: A Sunday dance in Montmartre, painted so that the sunlight never holds still.

lesson.text: A polka, slightly too fast. Shoes scraping on packed earth. A chair dragged back, a glass set down, forty conversations at once and somebody laughing over all of them. This painting makes no sound, of course. Yet most people who stand in front of it say they can nearly hear it.

The place is the Moulin de la Galette, an open-air dance garden on the hill of Montmartre, which in 1876 was still half village on the edge of Paris. On Sunday afternoons, working people climbed up there: seamstresses, shop clerks, florists, apprentices. They put on their best clothes and danced until evening.
“Moulin” means mill: a real windmill stood on the site. The family who owned it sold visitors a galette, a plain flat cake, with something to drink. The cake gave the dance hall its name.

Renoir was 35 and short of money. He rented a studio a few streets away and recruited his crowd from two groups: girls from the neighborhood, who agreed to pose, and his own friends, painters and writers, who had no choice. One of those friends is easy to pick out, thanks to a habit.
Someone in this crowd is smoking a long, thin pipe. Can you spot him?

spots.title: The pipe smoker
spots.text: Top hat, short beard, a white clay pipe between his fingers. He sits at the table on the right with two companions, half listening, eyes somewhere else.

lesson.text: The three men at that table belonged to Renoir's circle, two painters and a young writer, Georges Rivière. Rivière later described those weeks in a book, which is why we know so much about who posed. The man in the straw hat beside the smoker seems to hold a pencil: he may be the one taking notes.

Notice what Renoir refuses to do. An older painter would have built this scene around a hero: one couple, one face, with everyone else arranged around them. Here nobody is in charge. Your eye lands on a face, slides to a hat, jumps to a dress. That is exactly how you look around at a party.

spots.title: The dancers
spots.text: A woman in pink turns her face to us while her tall partner bends toward her. Tradition names them Margot, a favorite model, and a Cuban painter friend. They dance in the only clear patch of ground.

spots.title: The girl on the bench
spots.text: Striped dress, pink and blue, and a dreamy half smile aimed at someone outside the picture. She is said to be Estelle, the sister of one of Renoir's models.

spots.title: A hand on her shoulder
spots.text: A second woman in black leans over the girl and rests a hand on her. She listens to the men at the table. The two heads form the calm center of the storm.

spots.title: The glasses
spots.text: A bottle and tall glasses, a few fast strokes each. The reddish drink is usually said to be grenadine, a sweet syrup with water. An afternoon out did not have to be expensive.

spots.title: Mother and child
spots.text: In the lower left corner, a woman bends toward a small blond girl. Families came too. Renoir wanted the dance to look respectable and gentle, not wild.

spots.title: A small face
spots.text: Easy to miss: a child's round face looks out between the adults, at about the height of their elbows.

spots.title: The gas lamps
spots.text: Clusters of glass globes hang above the crowd. They are not lit yet. When evening comes, the dance will go on under gaslight.

lesson.text: The canvas measures about 131 by 175 centimeters (roughly 4 by 6 feet). According to Rivière, friends carried it from the studio to the garden and back on working days, and one windy afternoon it nearly flew away like a kite.

Why go to such trouble instead of painting indoors from sketches? Because the true subject was only available on site. The garden was planted with trees, and the afternoon sun came through the leaves in pieces. Renoir wanted those pieces, on every surface they touched.

lesson.title: Chasing the sun
lesson.text: Follow the light that falls through the leaves.

spots.title: A spotted jacket
spots.text: The man with his back to us wears a dark jacket, covered in pale round patches. They are not a pattern in the cloth. They are coins of sunlight that slipped between the leaves.

spots.title: A straw hat
spots.text: Where the sun hits it directly, the hat turns nearly white, with a ribbon of deep blue. The face under the brim stays in cool shade.

spots.title: The ground
spots.text: The beaten earth should be brown. Renoir paints it in pink, lilac and sky blue, with loose strokes that never settle. The floor itself seems to be dancing.

lesson.text: Something else is at work in those patches. The shadows are not black or brown, as painters had been taught to make them. They are blue and violet. Renoir and his friends had noticed that outdoors, shade picks up the color of the sky. Even the men's dark suits here are built from deep blues.
Impressionism in one idea: paint what the eye receives at a given moment, light and color first, and let the outlines take care of themselves.

Renoir showed the picture in 1877, at the third exhibition organized by the group of painters now called the Impressionists. Reactions were split. Some writers loved its cheerfulness. Others could not get past the blotches: to them, the light on the clothes looked like stains, and the faces looked unfinished.

The first owner was another painter. Gustave Caillebotte, who had family money, bought works from his struggling friends and left his collection to the French state when he died. That gift is why this canvas now belongs to a Paris museum.

Renoir also made a smaller version of the same scene. In 1990 it sold at auction for 78.1 million dollars, at the time one of the highest prices ever paid for a painting. A long way from grenadine and flat cake.

Montmartre is a district of Paris now, and the dance garden is long gone. The band packed up well over a century ago. On this canvas it is still about four o'clock on a Sunday, the sun is still coming through the leaves, and the polka has not finished.

quiz.question: What gave the Moulin de la Galette its name?
options: A flat cake sold at the mill
quiz.explanation: The owners of the windmill sold visitors a galette, a plain flat cake.

quiz.question: What are the pale round patches on the seated man's jacket?
quiz.explanation: Renoir painted the broken light that came through the trees.

quiz.question: What color are most shadows in this painting?
quiz.explanation: Outdoors, shade picks up the color of the sky.

quiz.question: Who was the first owner of the painting?
options: The owner of the dance hall
quiz.explanation: Caillebotte bought his friends' work and left it to the French state.

quiz.question: How is the crowd organized?
options: Around one heroic couple in the center
In strict rows, by social rank
quiz.explanation: The eye jumps from face to face, as it does at a real party.

quiz.question: Who posed for the figures?
options: Local girls and Renoir's own friends
Nobody, it was painted from imagination
quiz.explanation: Neighborhood girls agreed to pose, and his painter and writer friends filled the rest.

facts.text: A smaller version of this scene sold for 78.1 million dollars in 1990.
facts.explanation: It was one of the highest auction prices of its time.

facts.text: The gas lamps in the painting are lit, because the scene takes place at night.
facts.explanation: It is a sunny afternoon; the lamps are waiting for evening.

facts.text: The dancers at the Moulin de la Galette were mostly aristocrats.
facts.explanation: They were working people: seamstresses, clerks, florists, apprentices.
